mstts:express-as.prosody: Welcome to this journey where we take a closer look at how adversity can completely reshape our world—often when we least expect it. You know, those tough moments in life that seem to shake us to our very core? They have a way of challenging everything we think we know about ourselves. In No Pressure, No Diamonds: Mining for Gifts in Illness and Loss, Teri A. Dillion invites us to see illness and grief not just as something to survive, but as powerful forces that can spark transformation. What if, instead of simply enduring suffering, we could actually discover hidden gifts within it—like resilience, clarity, or a deeper sense of connection to ourselves and others? Together, we’ll explore how moments of loss—whether that’s a change in health or an emotional upheaval—can reveal strengths we never knew we had. Just like diamonds, which are formed under incredible pressure, our own hardships might hold the potential to uncover unexpected beauty and wisdom. As we move forward, let’s shift our focus from what’s been lost to what can be found inside those difficult experiences. This isn’t a solitary road; we’re in it together, finding compassion, wisdom, and gratitude along the way. Through vulnerability and courage, there’s a chance for real personal growth—and maybe, a whole new appreciation for the delicate beauty of life. So, let’s open ourselves to the idea that even the most challenging times can illuminate what truly matters, and set the stage for discovering the gifts hidden within adversity.

Chapter 1: When Life Changes Without Warning — The First Shock of Illness.
There’s a moment—sometimes so ordinary, you barely notice it—when everything quietly shifts. One minute, life is rolling along as usual: maybe you’re pouring your morning coffee, scrolling through messages, making plans for the day ahead. And then, out of nowhere, it all changes. Sometimes it’s a phone call. Sometimes it’s an odd ache you can’t explain, or a doctor’s concerned look that makes your stomach drop. Suddenly, life splits in two: before and after. Most of the time, that first sign of serious illness or loss doesn’t come with drama. It just sneaks in, a quiet sense that something’s off, even as the world outside keeps turning. But now, nothing feels certain.
In those first days of a health crisis, confusion and disbelief have a way of taking over. Picture yourself in a sterile exam room, fluorescent lights buzzing overhead. You’re listening as the doctor shares news that instantly changes your world—a diagnosis, a prognosis, a new reality you never planned for. Your mind races: Wasn’t I fine yesterday? You start replaying every single detail—every symptom, every choice, even wondering if you could somehow bargain your way back to the life you had just a moment ago.
For one woman, it all started with a fatigue she just couldn’t shake. She thought it was stress, or maybe just a busy week. But the signs kept coming: aches, strange bruises, a nagging sense that something deep inside was changing. When the diagnosis finally arrived, it was like she’d been dropped into a foreign country—no map, no language, and everything unfamiliar. The medical words felt overwhelming, the treatment options impossible to sort through. Even though friends and family tried to offer comfort, their words felt distant, like they couldn’t quite reach the depth of her fear.
During those first days, it’s so common to feel caught between denial and panic. You hope the doctors are wrong, that the test results got mixed up, that tomorrow you’ll wake up and everything will make sense again. But as reality begins to settle in, your whole world narrows. Suddenly, what mattered yesterday—traffic, deadlines, chores—just fades away. What really matters comes into crystal clear focus: the people who show up, the moments of unexpected kindness, the simple relief of taking a breath without pain.
Feeling isolated is almost inevitable in this new world. Even when you’re surrounded by loved ones, it’s easy to feel set apart—marked by something others can’t truly understand. Some people push themselves to keep up appearances, determined not to let illness define who they are. Others turn inward, overwhelmed by the weight of it all. The body becomes both battleground and teacher, forcing you to face your own vulnerability head-on.
And yet, even in the shock and uncertainty, tiny sparks of resilience begin to show up. Maybe it’s a nurse’s gentle touch, or a friend who just sits with you in silence. Maybe it’s the comfort of a favorite song playing in the background. These small moments offer brief relief from the storm. Over time, you start to realize that while the future is still unknown, there’s meaning to be found right here and now. The journey is only beginning, but already, the seeds of transformation are being planted—quietly, gently, in the space between fear and hope.

Chapter 2: Facing Fear and Uncertainty—Learning to Live With Not Knowing
After that first wave of shock settles, something new starts to take hold—the challenge of living with the unknown. You know, our minds are always searching for answers, timelines, and guarantees.
But illness? It rarely gives us that kind of clarity. Each day can bring a dozen new questions—Will this treatment actually work? How much is my life going to change? What if things never go back to the way they were?
Suddenly, the future, which once felt so carefully mapped out, starts to look like a blank page.
For many people, fear moves in and sticks around. It’s there in the middle of the night, in those long hours waiting on test results, or in the worried eyes of loved ones trying hard to stay strong. Some folks try to outrun it, filling every moment with research, chasing second opinions, or spinning through endless “what if” scenarios. Others just freeze, feeling overwhelmed by how big and unpredictable everything seems. There’s a real temptation to retreat into old routines, hoping that maybe, if you just keep doing what you’ve always done, nothing will really have to change.
I want to share a story. There was a man, newly diagnosed with a chronic illness, who threw himself into medical journals, convinced that if he learned enough, he’d somehow gain control. He memorized statistics, tracked every tiny symptom, and questioned his doctors about every detail. But here’s what happened—the more he learned, the more anxious he became.
Those numbers didn’t comfort him at all; they just made the journey ahead feel even more unpredictable. Finally, exhaustion forced him to stop. And in that quiet, he realized something important: certainty is kind of an illusion.
The only thing he could truly control was how he responded to each moment.
Others find a different way forward. They learn that fear can be softened—even if it never fully disappears—by connecting with others. Take the mother facing a life-changing diagnosis. She found herself at a support group, hesitant at first to share her story, worried she’d weigh others down. But as she listened to people who’d walked the same road, something changed. Their honesty gave her permission to face her own fears.
She discovered that being vulnerable wasn’t a weakness at all—it was a bridge to real understanding. And in opening up about her struggles, she found a kind of strength she didn’t realize she had.
Living with uncertainty takes a new kind of courage. It’s not the noisy kind where you’re fighting a battle, but more the quiet sort—showing up, day after day, even when you have no idea what tomorrow will bring. Some days, hope comes easily: the treatment helps, the pain fades, laughter bubbles up again. Other days, despair creeps in, and the weight of the future feels almost too much to carry. That’s when small rituals can help—a morning walk, your favorite book, or just chatting with a friend. These things don’t erase the fear, but they remind us: life keeps going, even when we’re living with uncertainty.
Over time, a lot of people start to see that not knowing isn’t really the enemy. In fact, it can be a teacher, nudging us toward a deeper trust in the present. That old urge to control everything slowly gives way to acceptance—not giving up, but recognizing that life is always changing.
And in that space, gratitude can actually grow. Not for the illness itself, but for the clarity it brings.
The things that matter most—love, connection, meaning—they shine even brighter against the unknown. And while the future remains unwritten, the present suddenly feels full of possibility.

Chapter 3: The Hidden Strength in Vulnerability—Letting Others In
As our journey moves forward, there’s something important that comes into focus—healing isn’t meant to be a solo act.
I know, we live in a world that celebrates independence and keeping a brave face. We’re taught to tough it out, to protect the people we care about from worry, to never let our guard down. But let’s be honest—trying to carry all that pain on your own? Eventually, it just gets too heavy.
Letting others in... now that’s a challenge. It means admitting you’re scared, asking for help, and allowing yourself to be seen—especially in those raw, unsteady moments. For a lot of us, that can feel like we’re somehow failing.
I remember a young professional who was used to having every detail of her life under control. Suddenly, she faced a tough diagnosis. She worried about being a burden, about losing her identity. But as her strength faded, she realized she couldn’t do it all alone. Friends dropped off meals, coworkers picked up her slack, and family sat with her through the long, restless nights. With every act of kindness, her walls started to come down, and she found a new kind of strength—the courage to receive.
These are the moments that really test—and transform—our relationships. Sometimes, people we expect to be there drift away, not sure how to handle the intensity. But then someone else surprises us, stepping up just when we need it most, offering presence instead of easy answers.
Imagine a father, who’d always been distant, sitting quietly at his daughter’s bedside. At first, it’s all small talk and silence. But as the hours tick by, something shifts. They start to share stories—old memories, regrets, dreams for the future. It’s not that the illness magically disappears, but somehow, it becomes a doorway to connection.
And here’s something else that happens—vulnerability makes room for self-compassion. So many people are surprised by just how harsh their own inner voice can be, always expecting perfection and rarely offering forgiveness. But when life throws you off course, there’s a chance to practice being gentle with yourself.
Like the woman recovering from surgery, frustrated by her slow progress. She’d beat herself up for needing help, for not bouncing back quickly enough. Then, a nurse quietly reminded her, “healing takes time.” That simple phrase became her anchor. Little by little, she learned to treat herself with the same kindness she’d offer anyone else.
Letting others in doesn’t mean giving up control. It’s about realizing that real strength and vulnerability—they aren’t opposites. In fact, they go hand in hand. Being willing to be seen, to ask for help, to admit you’re scared—these are acts of incredible courage. They open the door to true connection, to shared laughter and tears, to the kind of support that makes the journey a little bit lighter.
And as time goes on, many discover something beautiful—the relationships built during hardship often become the most meaningful of all. The folks who show up, who listen without judging, who offer their presence instead of quick fixes—those are the companions who help carry us through.
When you let others in, the burden gets lighter, and suddenly, the path ahead doesn’t feel quite so lonely.

Chapter 4—Finding Meaning in Suffering: The Gifts Hidden in Hardship.
As days slowly turn into weeks and months, you might notice something unexpected. Sure, the pain and uncertainty are still there, but alongside them, new insights quietly begin to surface.
People who’ve walked through illness or loss often talk about these surprising gifts—moments of clarity, gratitude, and personal growth that, strangely enough, only seem to appear on the other side of hardship.
Now, let’s be honest. In the beginning, the idea that suffering could hold any meaning at all just sounds impossible, doesn’t it? If given the choice, most of us would trade every lesson for a return to health, or for things to go back to the way they used to be.
But as time goes on, something changes. The sharp edges of pain start to soften, and you begin to notice subtle shifts inside. Priorities realign. The things that once felt urgent—like career ambitions, social status, or material comforts—suddenly don’t seem so important anymore. Instead, deeper values like kindness, presence, and authenticity begin to take root.
I remember hearing about a woman who, after months of exhausting treatment, started noticing beauty in the smallest things—a bird flitting outside her window, the gentle warmth of sunlight on her face, the sound of laughter drifting from the next room. These tiny moments, which she’d hardly noticed before, became her lifelines. Illness had stripped away all the noise, leaving only what mattered most. Gratitude, once just a word, became something she practiced every single day.
Others discover new sources of strength. Think about a man who always took pride in being self-sufficient. Suddenly, he’s forced to lean on others during a long recovery. At first, it feels like defeat. But as he lets himself accept help, he’s struck by the generosity of those around him. He learns to receive without feeling ashamed, and to trust that he’s truly worthy of care. That shift doesn’t just change his relationships—it reshapes how he sees himself.
For some, suffering sparks a deeper spiritual search. The need to find meaning becomes urgent. Old beliefs get questioned, new perspectives explored. Imagine a woman who’d never thought of herself as spiritual—she finds comfort in simple meditation and quiet prayer. She doesn’t find all the answers, but she discovers a sense of peace simply by letting go, and surrendering to something larger than herself.
These gifts aren’t always dramatic. Sometimes, they show up as a quiet resilience—a new ability to weather life’s storms, to adapt when everything shifts, or to hold onto hope even in the darkest moments. Over time, you realize resilience isn’t something you’re just born with. It’s built, bit by bit, in the fire of adversity, shaped by your willingness to keep going—even when the road ahead is hard to see.
When people look back, they almost never say they’d choose to go through that pain again. But many are surprised to find themselves changed for the better. They’re more compassionate, more present, more alive to the beauty and fragility of life. The gifts of suffering are hard-won, but they’re real. And in discovering them, the whole journey starts to take on a new kind of meaning.

Chapter 5. Redefining Identity: Who Am I Now?
After months, or even years, of living with illness or loss, there’s a question that starts to bubble up—one that’s really tough to ignore. Who am I now?
Think about all the labels and roles that used to define you—maybe you were a parent, a pro at your job, an athlete, or the go-to caretaker. But when life changes—when your body isn’t the same, relationships get shaken up, or your dreams get paused—those old roles might not fit anymore.
This process of redefining who you are? It’s rarely simple. There’s a real pull to hang on to the past, to grieve for the person you used to be. Imagine a teacher who, because of chronic pain, can’t be in her classroom anymore. She didn’t just lose her job—she lost that sense of purpose and belonging. For a while, she felt completely adrift, unsure where she fit in the world.
And then, there’s the outside pressure—friends and family, trying to help, saying things like, “Stay positive!” or “You’ll get back to normal.” But what if normal has changed? Pretending everything’s the same can actually leave you feeling even more alone.
Take a young man who used to love running. Suddenly, his body just can’t keep up. He tries to push through, hoping to get his old life back, but every setback is even more discouraging. It’s only when he allows himself to grieve that loss that he starts to picture new possibilities.
But you know what? In all this uncertainty, there’s also a spark of opportunity. When old identities fall away, you might find parts of yourself you never even noticed before. Like a woman who spent years caring for others—suddenly, she has time to paint, to write, to volunteer. She realizes her worth isn’t just about what she does for everyone else, but about who she is deep down.
Redefining your identity? That takes real courage. It’s about letting go of old stories, embracing change, and trusting that you can find new meaning. It’s not just about recovering—it’s about becoming.
For some, that means discovering new ways to make a difference—maybe by mentoring someone, sharing your story, or standing up for a cause. For others, it’s learning to rest, to accept help, or just to be.
Over time, you start to see that your identity isn’t stuck—it’s flexible, shaped by what you go through, the people you meet, and your willingness to grow. The person you become after illness or loss isn’t the same as before—and that’s not a bad thing. In fact, you might end up more yourself than ever—wiser, more compassionate, and clearer about what really matters.
This journey of redefining who you are? It’s ongoing. There’ll be setbacks, doubts, and moments of grief. But there’s also hope—a sense that, even through loss, new life can take root. The question shifts from, “Who was I?” to “Who am I becoming?” And when you land in that space, suddenly, anything feels possible.

Chapter 6: The Long Road—Endurance, Setbacks, and the Slow Work of Healing
Have you ever noticed how, after the dust settles from a big crisis, a different kind of exhaustion creeps in? It’s not just about being tired—it’s a deeper weariness that touches your spirit. The world seems to expect us to bounce back quickly, to snap back to “normal” as if nothing happened. But honestly, healing rarely works that way. It’s much more like a winding road, full of twists and unexpected turns.
The truth is, the hardest part isn’t always the initial drama. It’s what comes after. When the cards stop coming, when the casseroles run out, and everyone else moves on, that’s when the real work begins. Picture a man who, during his hospital stay, was surrounded by friends and family. But once he got home, the afternoons grew silent. The pain faded a bit, but the loneliness? That hit even harder. He missed the routine, the sense of purpose that came with his old life. Sure, some days he felt a little stronger—a short walk, a bit more energy. But then, out of nowhere, a setback would leave him convinced he’d never get back to where he was.
These long stretches are where true endurance is built. Most of us don’t realize just how much patience healing demands. There’s no shortcut, and no guarantee. Both mind and body take their time—usually, a lot more time than we’d like. Think about a woman recovering from surgery. Even tying her shoes, making breakfast, or climbing the stairs felt overwhelming at first. But slowly, she started to notice the little wins—less pain, a touch more strength, a laugh that felt genuine. That’s when she realized: healing isn’t just about the body. It’s about living with uncertainty, and celebrating every tiny bit of progress.
And setbacks? They’re just part of the journey. Maybe it’s a sudden fever, a tough scan, or a wave of sadness that knocks you back. In those moments, it’s easy to feel like all your progress has disappeared. But over time, you start to see that setbacks don’t erase the journey—they’re simply part of it. You learn to be kinder to yourself, to rest when you need it, and to ask for help without feeling guilty. This slow, steady work teaches us real humility, patience, and a deep respect for what our bodies can do.
In the quiet of these days, new routines begin to take shape. Maybe it’s a morning cup of tea, a favorite song playing, or a quick call with a friend. These small rituals become anchors, gentle reminders that, even if life looks different, it still goes on. The long road of recovery isn’t glamorous, but it’s where resilience grows—one day, and one small step at a time.

Chapter 7: Deepening Relationships—Love, Loss, and the Power of Presence.
As our journey unfolds, you might notice just how much deeper and more complex relationships become. Illness and loss have this remarkable way of stripping away all the layers—leaving only what’s truly real between us. Sometimes, those bonds grow even stronger, forged in the fires of adversity. But other times, they falter, unable to withstand the weight of what’s happening.
Imagine a couple who’s been married for decades. Suddenly, one of them falls seriously ill, and everything they thought they knew about their roles gets flipped upside down overnight. The caregiver becomes unsure and frustrated, while the one who’s sick feels guilty—worried about becoming a burden. In the beginning, there’s tension and resentment. But, as the weeks pass, something changes. They start finding new ways to communicate. Sometimes, they just sit together in silence. They even manage to find humor in the oddest moments—like the absurdities of hospital life. What was once routine love now becomes their lifeline. Isn’t it amazing how hardship can reveal what truly matters?
Of course, not every relationship survives this kind of strain. Some friends just… disappear. Maybe the reality of illness is too much for them. Others might offer empty platitudes or keep trying to “fix” what can’t really be fixed. Take the story of a young woman who used to be at the heart of her social circle. After her diagnosis, the invitations slowed down, texts started going unanswered, and she felt completely alone. But over time, she found new friends—people who understood the language of loss, who could sit with her in the dark and not try to pull her out before she was ready. Those fewer friendships became deeper and more honest than anything she’d known before.
Family dynamics shift, too. Old wounds can resurface, but so can opportunities for healing. Picture a son who’d barely spoken to his father for years. When he heard about his dad’s illness, he decided to reach out. Their first talks were awkward—filled with silence and regret. But as they began sharing memories and fears, something new began to grow. It wasn’t about fixing the past, but about being present, offering forgiveness, and giving each other a fresh start.
Here’s something to really pay attention to: presence—just being there—can be the greatest gift of all. Most people don’t realize how powerful it is to simply show up. You don’t need grand words or perfect advice. Sometimes, just sitting quietly, listening, or holding someone’s hand speaks louder than anything you could say. In the end, it’s not the big gestures that carry us through. It’s those steady, quiet acts of love that mean everything.

Chapter 8: The Unexpected Gifts — Wisdom, Perspective, and a New Way of Seeing.
Over time, pain’s sharp edges start to soften. And then, something almost magical happens — the world changes before your eyes. Colors seem brighter, moments feel richer, and life itself becomes more precious.
If you talk to people who’ve made it through illness or loss, you’ll often hear about a wisdom they never could’ve learned any other way.
There’s this man who survived a near-fatal accident. He said that, for the first time, he really noticed sunlight slipping through the leaves, or the way his children’s laughter filled the room, or even just the taste of fresh bread. These little things he’d always brushed past suddenly felt... miraculous. He realized that suffering had stripped away all the background noise, leaving only what truly mattered.
Others discover new passions. Take the woman who was once completely absorbed in her career. During her recovery, she stumbled into painting — and it changed everything. She found comfort in color and texture, in turning pain into something beautiful. Her art became a way to process her experience, to share her story without having to say a word.
And then there are people who become more compassionate, more tuned in to what others are going through. Like the nurse who, after surviving cancer herself, realized she was connecting with her patients on a whole new level. She knew their fears and understood their vulnerability in ways she never had before. Her presence alone became a comfort — not because she had all the answers, but because she knew how to truly listen.
The gifts that come from adversity aren’t always easy to spot. Sometimes, they show up as a quiet confidence — a sense that, after surviving the worst, you can take on whatever comes next. Other times, they reveal themselves in the smallest pleasures: savoring a good meal, letting go of old grudges, or feeling a deeper sense of purpose.
Most of us would never choose the hard things we’ve faced. But it’s surprising, isn’t it, how often people find themselves changed for the better — wiser, more present, and somehow, more alive.
The world may still be uncertain, but now, it’s also more beautiful than ever before.

Chapter 9: Giving Back—Turning Pain Into Purpose
As the healing journey unfolds, a new question often comes up: What now?
For many, the answer is giving back—taking what they've been through, and using it to help someone else. That pain turns into empathy. Suddenly, it becomes a bridge to people who are still struggling.
Take the story of a man who lost his wife to illness. He started volunteering at a hospice center, even though he worried that being surrounded by suffering would be overwhelming. But what he found surprised him. Just being there—listening, holding a hand, simply sitting with others in their pain—brought comfort.
He didn’t need to have all the answers. His presence alone was enough. And in supporting others, he found a purpose that gently eased his own grief.
Others choose to share their stories, breaking the silence that often surrounds illness and loss. Think about a young woman who once felt ashamed of her diagnosis. Eventually, she began speaking at schools and community centers, opening up about her journey—her fears, setbacks, and even the unexpected gifts along the way.
Her honesty inspired others to open up too, to seek help, and to realize they weren’t alone after all.
Some people go even further, becoming advocates and working to change the systems that once let them down. Imagine a mother, frustrated by the lack of support for families facing chronic illness. She launched a nonprofit, determined to offer resources and build a community. Driven by her own experience, her efforts blossomed into something much bigger—a movement, a beacon of hope for so many others.
But giving back doesn’t need to be something big or official. Sometimes, it’s as simple as reaching out to a friend who’s hurting, offering a warm meal, a ride, or just a few kind words.
These small acts of kindness become a way to honor what’s been lost, and to find meaning within the pain.
When people turn pain into purpose, something powerful happens. They discover a new sense of agency. They’re no longer defined by what happened to them—but by what they choose to do next.
The journey isn’t over, but now, it’s filled with new meaning and hope.

Chapter 10: Living Forward—Embracing Change and the Ongoing Journey
You know, there comes a moment when the past just doesn’t have the same grip on you anymore. The scars are still there, of course, but they’re not the whole story. Life moves forward—not despite everything that’s happened, but because of it.
Picture this—a woman, years after her diagnosis, finally planning that trip she’d always dreamed about. She’s careful, sure, and she knows her limits, but she’s stopped letting fear call the shots. She understands her life will never look exactly like it did before, but that doesn’t mean it can’t be good. In fact, it’s still full of possibility.
Others find themselves pulled toward new adventures. Think about a man who, after a career that once defined him, takes up gardening during his recovery. He finds real joy in the slow, patient work of tending plants, watching things grow and change. That garden becomes a kind of mirror for his own life—there are setbacks and surprises, but also beauty and renewal.
Living forward means embracing change, letting go of old expectations, and staying open to whatever comes next. It’s not about forgetting what happened. Instead, it’s about weaving the past into your life—carrying the lessons, the wisdom, and the hard-earned resilience into a brand-new chapter.
Most of us don’t realize just how much we’ve changed until we look back. The fears that once felt so overwhelming now seem smaller, somehow. The pain? It’s still there, but it’s not the headline anymore. In its place, there’s this steady strength, a sense of possibility, and a willingness to keep moving forward.
The journey of healing and transformation is always ongoing. Sure, there’ll be new challenges, new losses, and new joys. But if you’ve walked this path, you know you’re capable of facing whatever comes. You’ve mined diamonds from the pressure, and you carry them with you—gifts that were hard-won, but deeply treasured.

As we wrap up, let’s take a moment to really honor how far you’ve come. When you’ve faced illness or loss, you know deep down that life shifts in ways you never expected. People might say, “Just move on,” but you and I know—it’s not about forgetting. It’s about carrying those hard-earned lessons with you, letting them shape the way you show up, love, and connect to the world around you.
So, as you keep going, here are a few gentle reminders to hold close:
Healing isn’t a straight line. There’ll be ups and downs, and that’s part of the process—not a sign you’re failing.
Simple moments of presence and kindness? They matter way more than finding the perfect words.
Being vulnerable doesn’t make you weak—it’s where real strength is born.
You might stumble across meaning in places you’d never expect, even when things feel tough.
When you share your story, honestly, you could become a lifeline for someone else who needs it.
Giving back—even in small ways—can turn pain into hope and give your journey new purpose.
Some relationships will change. But trust me, new connections can bring surprising joy and depth.
The person you’re becoming through adversity? You’re not less whole. If anything, you’re more.
When you open up to change, you invite new growth—and possibilities you might not have dreamed of.
And above all, you are not alone. So many others have walked this path before you and found their way.
Here’s what this means for you: there’s no single roadmap for healing. No “right way” to move through loss or illness. The diamonds you carry—your resilience, your wisdom, your compassion—those are yours to keep, no matter what comes next. Some days will feel heavy, and that’s okay. Let yourself rest, grieve, and celebrate even the smallest of victories.
And when you need support, reach out. When you’re able, offer it to someone else.
Life after hardship isn’t about going back to who you were—it’s about becoming who you’re meant to be. You are shaped, but never defined, by what you’ve lived through.
So, trust in your own strength. Know that each step forward—no matter how small—is proof of your courage. The gifts you’ve found in the dark will light your way, and maybe even help someone else find theirs.
Keep going. The world needs the diamonds only you can offer.
